vignette:
David has always believed in the integrity of systems. As an architect, he finds deep satisfaction in the logic of a well-designed structure-the way a load-bearing wall distributes weight, the precise angle of a roofline to shed water, the seamless integration of form and function. For twenty-five years, his world has been one of blueprints and calculations, a place where careful planning could mitigate almost any risk. His life with his wife, Sarah, was built on the same principles: stable, predictable, and secure.

That foundation cracked nine months ago, on a Tuesday morning that smelled of fresh-cut lumber and curing concrete. He was doing a walkthrough at the new municipal library project, a design he was particularly proud of. It was a bright, clear day. He was on the third-floor mezzanine, discussing a wiring conduit with the foreman, when a shout cut through the rhythmic din of construction. It wasn't a warning shout; it was a sound of pure, helpless terror.

David looked up, following the foreman's gaze. High above, against the brilliant blue sky, a young man-a scaffolder named Leo, barely twenty-was falling. For a fraction of a second that David's mind has replayed a thousand times, the boy seemed to hang in the air. David saw the panicked look on his face, the way his arms flailed for something that wasn't there. Then came the impact. It was not a loud sound, but a dense, sickening thud that seemed to absorb all other noise on the site. A terrible silence followed, broken only by the foreman's choked whisper, "Oh, God."

In the immediate aftermath, David was a model of professional composure. He spoke with the paramedics, the police, the OSHA investigators. He answered questions with a calm, detached precision, describing sightlines and scaffolding anchor points. He told Sarah he was fine, just shaken. He went back to the office the next day, believing that the familiar logic of his work would be a bulwark against the chaos of what he'd seen.

But the system was compromised. The image of Leo's fall began to intrude at random moments. He'd be reviewing a set of elevations, and instead of seeing the clean lines of a building, he'd see the trajectory of a body against the sky. The memory was a perfect, terrible photograph, and it would flash behind his eyes without warning, causing his breath to catch in his throat.

Sleep offered no escape. He'd jolt awake in a cold sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs, the thud of the impact echoing in his ears. Sarah would stir beside him, asking if he was okay, but he'd just stare at the ceiling, unable to explain the feeling that the room was tilting, that the floor wasn't solid beneath him.

His work, once his sanctuary, became a minefield. The percussive blast of a nail gun would make him flinch so violently he'd spill his coffee. He started avoiding site visits, sending his junior partner instead, making excuses about meetings he had to attend. He found himself unable to stand near the windows in the high-rise offices he'd designed, a profound and unfamiliar fear of heights gripping him. The pride he once felt looking at a finished project was replaced by a gnawing anxiety, a hyper-focus on every potential point of failure.

He has grown distant from Sarah, building a wall of silence between them. His irritability is a constant presence in their home; he snaps over trivial things, like a misplaced T-square or the volume of the television. He knows she's worried. He sees it in the way she watches him when she thinks he isn't looking. But the words to explain what's happening are locked away, buried under a layer of guilt he can't rationalize. He wasn't on the scaffold, he didn't sign off on the faulty harness, yet the thought persists: *I was in charge of the building. It happened in my space.* The world, which once felt so ordered and subject to design, now feels fragile and treacherous, and he no longer trusts the plans.
